hops.title: You can partly unboil an egg
hops.text: Everyone knows you can't unboil an egg. In 2015, Tom Yuan, Gregory Weiss, Colin Raston and their colleagues tried anyway. They cooked hen egg whites at 90 °C for twenty minutes, dissolved the rubbery white in urea, the same chemical Anfinsen used, and diluted it. Then they spun it at 5,000 revolutions per minute in a tilted glass tube. The thin film of spinning liquid helped tangled chains of the egg-white enzyme lysozyme refold, and within five minutes the enzyme worked again. They brought back one enzyme, not a breakfast, so their 2015 Ig Nobel Prize in Chemistry called it a recipe to "partially un-boil an egg."

sources.citation: Yuan TZ, Ormonde CFG, Kudlacek ST, et al. (2015). Shear-stress-mediated refolding of proteins from aggregates and inclusion bodies. ChemBioChem 16(3):393-396.
Improbable Research. Ig Nobel Prize winners, 2015 Chemistry Prize.

image.caption: Cooking tangles egg-white proteins, but under the right conditions some lysozyme refolds and works again.

hops.afterHeading: Helices and sheets: the backbone bonds to itself
hops.title: Stretch a wet hair from helix to sheet
hops.text: Take a shed hair from your hairbrush, soak it in tap water for a minute, and stretch it slowly between your fingers. It gives and lengthens before it snaps. Hair is mostly keratin, whose chains coil into alpha helices. Stretching wet horsehair, Laurent Kreplak and colleagues found in 2004 that the helices start to unravel at about 5 percent stretch. Above about 20 percent, the pulled-out chains line up into beta sheets. In one run, a wet fiber reached about 53 percent stretch just before it broke. William Astbury first saw this switch around 1930, as a change in the X-ray patterns of stretched hair and wool.

sources.citation: Kreplak L, Doucet J, Dumas P, Briki F (2004). New aspects of the alpha-helix to beta-sheet transition in stretched hard alpha-keratin fibers. Biophysical Journal 87(1):640-647.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: Two hands stretching a single wet hair over a bathroom sink beside a wooden hairbrush.
image.caption: Stretch wet hair far enough and its keratin helices unravel into beta sheets.

hops.title: Water bears survive drying with floppy proteins
hops.text: Tardigrades, the tiny eight-legged water bears, can dry out completely and revive when water returns, a trick that has puzzled biologists for more than 250 years. Some drying-tolerant creatures rely on the sugar trehalose, yet in one well-studied tardigrade, Thomas Boothby and colleagues found no gene for an enzyme needed to make it. Instead, they reported in 2017, drying turned up genes for several tardigrade-specific disordered proteins. Floppy in water, some of these proteins set into a glass-like solid when dried in the lab, which the team proposed protects cells. Yeast given just one of these genes survived drying up to about a hundred times better.

sources.citation: Boothby TC, Tapia H, Brozena AH, et al. (2017). Tardigrades use intrinsically disordered proteins to survive desiccation. Molecular Cell 65(6):975-984.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A plump tardigrade on green moss beside a dewdrop, with a faint glassy sheen.
image.caption: Some water bear proteins set into a glass-like solid in lab tests, which may help water bears survive drying.

audio.title: A perfect egg, a folding game and a faster insulin
audio.transcript:
Protein shapes sound abstract until they turn up at breakfast, in a video game, and in a medicine. Here are three true stories.

Start in a lab in Naples, with a problem every cook knows. Egg white and egg yolk set at different temperatures. For a firmly set white, the researchers aimed for around eighty-five degrees Celsius. The yolk is at its creamy best around sixty-five. Around sixty-five degrees, one egg-white protein, ovotransferrin, starts to thicken the white, but in the researchers' low-temperature egg the white stayed runny. Boil it hard, and the yolk turns into a solid paste. So in twenty twenty-five, Emilia Di Lorenzo, Ernesto Di Maio and their colleagues tried something odd. They moved a raw egg, still in its shell, back and forth between boiling water at one hundred degrees and lukewarm water at thirty degrees. Two minutes in each pot, eight rounds, thirty-two minutes in all. That rhythm set the white and left the yolk creamy. It is a lot of pot-swapping for one egg. The short hot bursts heated the white enough to set it, while the yolk stayed cooler and creamy.

The second story is a puzzle that beat the experts for over a decade. A monkey retrovirus makes a small enzyme, a protease just one hundred fourteen amino acids long. For more than ten years, crystallographers could not solve its crystal structure, even with models of it from another experimental method. In a study published in twenty eleven, researchers handed the problem to players of Foldit, an online game about folding proteins, played mostly by people with little or no training in biochemistry. The organizers gave them starting models chosen so they would not get stuck in a dip on the energy landscape. Then three teammates in the Foldit Contenders Group, playing under the names spvincent, grabhorn and mimi, passed the virtual chain back and forth. One reworked the backbone strands. One repacked the oily side chains in the hydrophobic core. One tucked in a loose loop. During a three-week competition, they built a model good enough for the scientists to solve the structure at last.

The third story is a medicine. Insulin is a small hormone made of two chains. In the vial, with zinc present, regular human insulin packs into clusters of six insulin molecules. After an injection, those clusters have to come apart into single molecules before the hormone moves into the blood as fast as it can, and that slows regular insulin down. So researchers made insulin lispro by swapping two neighbors near the end of the B chain. Proline at position twenty-eight and lysine at position twenty-nine trade places. That small flip removes two oily contacts and weakens two hydrogen bonds where two insulin molecules meet. Each molecule still works at full strength, and with zinc and a preservative it still packs into clusters of six in the vial. But once the preservative drifts away after the injection, those clusters are thought to fall apart straight into single, active molecules. Two neighbors trade places at the edge where molecules touch, and the medicine starts working sooner.
